judge.summary: Continuing the most recent winning line (shorter S-layer sliding window -> cheaper attention -> more optimizer updates), the agent changed exactly one line in train.py so that the S-layer window becomes 128 instead of 256, i.e. `short_window = long_window // 8` -> `long_window // 16` (with sequence_len = 2048 this yields 128), committed it, and ran the experiment. The run succeeded (no crash) and produced val_bpb = 1.007476 (peak_vram 26.0 GB, 1966 steps), which is a 0.000221 improvement over the current best of 1.007697 but well below the required 0.0005 margin, so the harness discards it as not a confirmed improvement.
judge.feedback: This was not a code bug: the one-line edit exactly implements the stated 256->128 window change, and the run is valid. The error is in the experiment-selection reasoning. The sliding-window line had already plateaued: by the time the S-window is 256, S-layer attention is a small share of a GEMM-dominated step, so halving it again saves almost no step time, and the extra updates it buys do not compensate for losing long-range context in the 5 S layers. The agent explicitly noted 'the gains may diminish' but still spent its single run on an extrapolation whose expected gain (~0.0002, inside the ~0.0002 measurement noise) was below the 0.0005 keep-threshold. Because only ONE experiment is allowed per session, betting it on a near-no-op was the decisive mistake; the agent should have recognized the diminishing returns and instead targeted a bottleneck with expected gain above 0.0005 (e.g. a GEMM/optimizer-side change or a different architectural knob) rather than continuing a line that had already bottomed out at window 256.
